paras: The threatened lynching of Harry Bell and Fannie Shelby took place at Batavia, Illinois, on the night of August 24, 1903, when a crowd of white townspeople surrounded the jail holding the two Black picnickers from Chicago and officers secretly moved them to the county jail at Geneva. The pair had been taken from a picnic train after picnickers were accused of beating a white woman and the city marshal. White papers across the country ran it as a lynching prevented, while the two Black papers that covered it did not mention the crowd at the jail.

The congregations of Quinn Chapel and Bethel Church of Chicago held a picnic at Mill Creek, two miles south of Batavia, attended by about 3,000 people by the wire's count and nearly 2,000 by another account. According to the wire, picnickers occupied the lawn of Mrs. George Burton, and when she ordered them off she was 'repeatedly struck by two of the negro women.' The Chicago Broad Ax said instead that one woman struck her after she objected to picnickers plucking her flowers.

City Marshal William Kelley (or Kelly) arrested two women, the wire said, but a crowd of 200 picnickers freed them and left him unconscious. The Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican said deputies then took Kelley to the picnic grounds to identify the attackers, followed by thirty townsmen 'armed with rifles and shotguns', and that 'the blood of the Batavia people was up.' When no one could be identified, the officers decided to stop the picnic train and called Sheriff Robert Burke of Kane County from Geneva.

The sheriff's posse took William Allen, Harry Bell and Fanny Shelby from the train at Batavia 'after a desperate battle in the railway coach and on the depot platform.' The Broad Ax, relying on what 'the officers claim', said the man and woman 'resisted arrest' and were 'severely clubbed by the Sheriff.' Bell and Shelby were held in the Batavia jail until 'a large crowd of citizens' gathered, and were then removed to Geneva 'to prevent a possible lynching'; Allen was later released. The Marshalltown paper said the two 'were saved from a mob, which threatened to storm the jail.'

No report of a hearing or trial of Bell or Shelby, or of action against the crowd at the jail, appears in the coverage. Two weeks later the Broad Ax reported that Bethel's pastor, Rev. Abraham Lincoln Murray, told his congregation the picnic had cleared more than $450 despite the drinking and fighting there.

Most white papers carried one wire story datelined Chicago, August 24, which ran the next day from Birmingham to Salt Lake City and in weeklies into September. Some headlines stressed the threat, such as 'CHICAGO NEGROES ARE ALMOST LYNCHED' in Savannah and 'GIVE MOB THE SLIP' in the Bemidji Daily Pioneer, while the Indianapolis Journal called the pair 'Two Members of a Disorderly Crowd from Chicago.' The Marshalltown paper told the story from the townspeople's side under 'WENCHES ATTACK WHITE LADY' and called the armed volunteers a 'rescue party'.

Weekly digests compressed it further, the Colfax Gazette saying the pair were 'accused of assaulting a white woman with their fists' and the Belding Banner writing of 'a desperate battle with would-be lynchers'. In Louisiana, the New Iberia Enterprise reprinted an editorial claiming the militia 'had to be called out' and calling the episode 'race hatred for you with a vengeance', to accuse Northern papers of a double standard.

Among Black papers, the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate reprinted a white dispatch under 'COLORED PICNICKERS ENGAGE IN A RIOT' without comment. The Chicago Broad Ax ran its own piece, 'MEN AND WOMEN OF THE TENDERLOIN DISTRICT', blaming 'tough or desperate characters' at the picnic for bringing 'disgrace and reproach on all decent Afro-Americans.'

The wire and the Broad Ax placed the events on Monday, August 24, but the Marshalltown account said the train was stopped 'Sunday night'. Accounts also differed on whether one or two women struck Mrs. Burton and on how many attacked the marshal, and every version came from the townspeople and officers. Only the Louisiana editorial mentioned the militia, and only the Savannah Morning News said the prisoners went to 'Clinton'.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Harry Bell and Fannie Shelby
bases: Bell and Shelby, two Black picnickers under arrest, were removed from the Batavia jail 'to prevent a possible lynching' after a crowd of white citizens gathered and, in one account, threatened to storm it (A1, A2, A3).
No one was killed: a crowd gathered at the jail to punish two Black prisoners accused of assault, but officers removed them to Geneva (A1, A2, A3); it was a threatened lynching, not a lynching.

The crowd at the jail and the removal to Geneva are reported in the Chicago wire (A1, A2) and in the separately written Marshalltown account (A3); the arrests and the earlier clashes are also reported in a second dispatch reprinted by a Black weekly (A15) and in the Broad Ax (A22), which do not mention the crowd at the jail.

accounts.label: Chicago wire
accounts.gist: Picnickers took over Mrs. Burton's lawn and two women struck her; 200 freed them from Marshal Kelley; a posse of forty-five took three from the train after a 'desperate battle'; a crowd at the jail led officers to remove Bell and Shelby to Geneva.

accounts.label: Marshalltown dispatch (townspeople's and officers' version)
accounts.gist: Two women beat Mrs. Burton and fifty or more beat and kicked the marshal; deputies and thirty armed citizens went to the picnic grounds; a mob 'threatened to storm the jail' and the pair were saved by officers.

accounts.label: Second dispatch reprinted by a Black weekly
accounts.gist: A woman picking flowers set off a 'riot'; the marshal was stoned; Shelby and Bell were taken from the train 'under the rifles of the sheriff's deputies'; no crowd at the jail is mentioned.

accounts.label: Black Chicago editor
accounts.gist: One woman struck Mrs. Burton and escaped after picnickers beat the officer; the sheriff searched the train and, so the officers claimed, found the pair in the last car and clubbed them; no crowd at the jail is mentioned.

framing.detail: The wire ran under headlines such as 'NEGROES LOCKED IN JAIL TO PREVENT A LYNCHING' and 'CHICAGO NEGROES ARE ALMOST LYNCHED', telling the story as one of Black disorder ended by officers.
The Marshalltown paper headlined 'WENCHES ATTACK WHITE LADY', wrote that 'the blood of the Batavia people was up', and cast the armed townsmen as a 'rescue party'.
A Louisiana editorial said the townspeople would have lynched excursionists over a plucked flower and called it 'race hatred', to answer Northern critics of the South.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate reprinted a white dispatch, 'COLORED PICNICKERS ENGAGE IN A RIOT', without comment.

The Broad Ax condemned the picnickers' conduct and the church that profited from it, while noting the sheriff's clubbing and that the woman's guilt was still to be proven in court; it did not mention the threat at the jail.
